extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for forming and assessing inductive inferences and laws of nature: how to generalize from observed instances, when enumeration suffices, the role of uniformity, and how to prefer, verify, and relate different inductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction properly so called is 'Generalization from Experience' — inferring from some individual instances in which a phenomenon is observed that it occurs in all instances of a certain class; namely, in all which 'resemble' the former in what are regarded as the material circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an inductive claim, check that the inference moves from observed instances to unobserved instances of a class defined by relevant (material) similarities; ensure the extension is limited to cases that 'resemble' in the material circumstances invoked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish material from immaterial circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid induction requires identifying which circumstances are 'material' (relevant) and which are 'immaterial' to the phenomenon; the inference applies only to instances resembling in the material circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments must examine whether the author has justified which factors count as material. Mill notes 'we are not yet ready to point out' how to distinguish them, so explicit argument or empirical testing about relevance is required rather than assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of the course of nature (ultimate axiom)
rubrics_metrics.description: All inductions rest on the principle that the course of nature is uniform — that there are parallel cases and that what happens once will, under sufficient similarity of circumstances, happen again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat uniformity as a necessary presupposition (the ultimate major premise) of inductive reasoning. Critiques should ask whether the inference covertly depends on an unwarranted uniformity claim and whether that presupposition is itself plausible in the domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: The uniformity axiom is itself an induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposition that the course of nature is uniform is itself a generalization from experience and not an a priori axiom; it derives from prior, perhaps more obvious, generalizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When invoking uniformity as justification, recognize it's not a primitive proof; demand grounding in prior reliable generalizations. Be wary of treating uniformity as self-evident authority in an argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate invention/colligation with induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The introduction of a new conception (invention, colligation, explication) is a different mental operation from induction; inventing a new concept or collating facts does not by itself constitute inductive proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a purported 'induction' is merely conceptual framing or descriptive colligation. Good work should separate creative hypothesis-generation from the distinct task of proving a generalization by evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductio per enumerationem simplicem is usually insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple enumeration (inferring a general truth because every known instance agrees and no contradicting instance is known) is a loose form of induction and generally inadequate for science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the author relies solely on enumeration; such inference is only acceptable when there is reason to believe that any contrary instance would have been observed (i.e., assurance that negative instances would have been known). Mill's examples: 'all swans are white' fails despite unanimous known instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of assurance that contrary instances would have been noticed
rubrics_metrics.description: Before concluding universal truth from never-seen-contrary instances, one must have reason to believe that if contrary instances existed they would have been discovered; lacking this assurance, enumeration is weak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the domain is one in which negative instances are likely to have been observed; only in such cases can single or few observations be elevated to general laws (e.g., carefully-executed chemical experiment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer inductions reducible to stronger, simpler uniformities
rubrics_metrics.description: An induction gains strength if it can be deduced from simpler, better-established uniformities (laws); complex uniformities that are results of simpler laws are less fundamental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favour explanations that reduce observed regularities to a minimal set of simple, general assumptions ('fewest and simplest assumptions'). Assess whether the claimed law can be shown to follow from more general laws (example: Kepler's laws as consequences of Newtonian mechanics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification desirable even for deduced results
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when a result follows deductively from accepted laws, specific verification by experience is desirable and may be indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept purely theoretical deduction without empirical confirmation when practicable; expect authors to provide or cite verification even for predictions derived from general laws (Mill's Torricellian example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey past inductions to identify reliably invariable uniformities
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific induction requires a prior survey of the inductions to which mankind have been led in unscientific practice, to learn which kinds of uniformities have been found invariable and which vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When justifying an inductive method or claim, the author should situate it among known regularities and explain why the case at hand belongs to a class whose uniformities are historically reliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve conflicts by preferring stronger inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: If an induction conflicts with stronger inductions or with conclusions correctly deduced from them, the weaker must give way unless the stronger were overgeneralized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluation, identify the hierarchy of inductions: prefer those with broader, stronger support; if conflict exists, require re-examination of scope and universality claims before accepting the weaker claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class-plausibility and domain-specific constancy determine credence
rubrics_metrics.description: The credibility of a universal claim depends on the degree of constancy in that class of phenomena (e.g., anatomical relations are more plausibly invariant than animal coloration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess inductive claims against domain-specific expectations about variability; use background empirical knowledge about how changeable features are in that domain to calibrate confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active 'interrogation' (experiment) over passive observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Passive acceptance of presented facts ('mera palpatio') is inferior to the scientific mode of actively seeking the necessary facts — 'interrogating nature' — to justify a safe conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value methodologies that design experiments or seek out potential counterinstances rather than relying solely on passive accumulation of concordant observations. Criticize claims that do not attempt to test for possible exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unravel complex uniformities into constituent regularities
rubrics_metrics.description: The apparent general regularity of nature is a complex web of partial regularities; scientific progress consists in resolving complex uniformities into simpler independent laws (tracing separate 'threads').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the work attempts to decompose complex phenomena into simpler causal regularities; prize analyses that show how a complex regularity results from simpler, independently supported laws.
